query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, stress–strain behavior, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior at elevated temperatures remain insufficiently understood. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain these responses? Define a controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline state, the temperature and response limits within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the HfNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy, the unusual stress–strain, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior at elevated temperatures arise because of a thermally induced shift in the dominant dislocation mechanism from screw-controlled to edge-controlled glide. This transition is mediated by the inherent severe lattice distortion of the alloy that alters dislocation core structures and mobility.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single‐phase BCC structured HfNbTaTiZr alloy (as‐cast/homogenized) with typical lattice distortion effects inherent to refractory HEAs.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or compression tests) with in situ characterization (e.g., in situ neutron diffraction or TEM) at elevated temperatures.
generation.conditions: Testing conducted in a temperature range of approximately 700°C to 1400°C under controlled strain rates that allow thermally activated dislocation processes to be captured.
generation.structural_mediator: The high degree of lattice distortion in the alloy alters dislocation core energies, promoting a temperature-dependent change from a screw dislocation‐dominated regime to one where edge dislocation motion prevails.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, screw dislocations—strongly hindered by lattice distortion—dominate deformation, leading to high yield strength and limited elastic softening. As temperature rises, thermal activation reduces the energy barrier for edge dislocation motion; this shift promotes a plateau in yield stress and modified elastic responses along with subtle variations in thermal expansion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to room temperature, elevated-temperature tests (700°C–1400°C) should reveal: (1) a yield strength plateau or moderate softening rather than continuous decline, (2) elastic moduli that decrease less steeply than expected from pure thermal softening, (3) measurable evidence (via microscopy) of an increasing relative density of edge dislocations versus screw dislocations, and (4) thermal expansion behavior that deviates from standard metals due to changes in interatomic spacing.
generation.baseline: Room temperature mechanical behavior and dislocation structure of the same HfNbTaTiZr alloy, where screw dislocations are expected to dominate.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is posited to govern behavior in the intermediate elevated-temperature regime (approximately 700°C to 1400°C). Outside of this range (e.g., at cryogenic or ultra-high temperatures), other deformation mechanisms may predominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature at which the transition occurs and the quantitative influence of lattice distortion on both elastic properties and dislocation type ratios remain to be precisely determined. Minor compositional inhomogeneities could also influence the observed behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ TEM and neutron diffraction experiments on homogenized HfNbTaTiZr specimens during mechanical loading at gradually increasing temperatures (from 700°C up to 1400°C). Use quantitative dislocation analysis to track the relative densities and types of dislocations, and simultaneously record complete stress–strain curves and measure elastic moduli and thermal expansion coefficients.
measurements: Dislocation type counts (screw vs edge) via in situ TEM/neutron diffraction
Yield and flow stresses based on stress–strain curves
Elastic modulus values at various temperatures
Thermal expansion coefficients derived from in situ measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental data do not show a significant increase in the proportion of edge dislocations with temperature, or if the yield strength and elastic moduli do not exhibit the predicted plateau or moderate softening behavior in the 700°C–1400°C range relative to the room-temperature baseline, the hypothesis that a thermally induced transition from screw to edge dislocation dominated deformation is responsible for the observed behavior will be rejected.

Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Conclusions: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen

Microstructure and Room Temperature Mechanical Properties of Different 3 and 4 Element Medium Entropy Alloys from HfNbTaTiZr System

Abstract: Refractory high entropy alloys (HEA) are promising materials for high temperature applications. This work presents investigations of the room temperature tensile mechanical properties of selected 3 and 4 elements medium entropy alloys (MEA) derived from the HfNbTaTiZr system. Tensile testing was combined with fractographic and microstructure analysis, using scanning electron microscope (SEM), wavelength dispersive spectroscope (WDS) and X-Ray powder diffraction (XRD). The 5 element HEA alloy HfNbTaTiZr exhibits the best combination of strength and elongation while 4 and 3 element MEAs have lower strength. Some of them are ductile, some of them brittle, depending on microstructure. Simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr in the alloy resulted in a significant reduction of ductility caused by reduction of the BCC phase content. Precipitation of Ta rich particles on grain boundaries reduces further the maximum elongation to failure down to zero values.

Conclusions: Investigations of mechanical properties and microstructure of different MEAs derived

Edge-dislocation-induced ultrahigh elevated-temperature strength of HfMoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: ABSTRACTOver 150 refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) have been proposed in the last decade. Early alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW still show an unparalleled yield strength of approximately 400 MPa at 1600°C. However, RHEAs with even elevated high-temperature strength are necessary in aerospace vehicles and nuclear reactors to cope with advanced technology in the future. Here, solid-solution strengthening calculation and melting point prediction are combined to design single-phase RHEA for attaining ultrahigh strength at 1600°C. The results show that Hf0.5MoNbTaW and HfMoNbTaW alloys after fully homogeneous treatment at 2100°C for 2 h reveal a homogenous body-centered cubic phase. HfMoNbTaW alloy exhibits a yield strength of 571 MPa at 1600°C, much higher than that of MoNbTaVW (477 MPa). It is found that a plateau of strength occurs from 800°C to 1200°C, which is important for raising the strength level of RHEAs at high temperatures.
